# Short stature

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Surgery > Pediatric surgery > Short stature*

[Original Article Link](/library/c40aRT)

---

## Summary

Short stature (dwarfism) in children is defined as a height that is at least two <u>standard deviations</u> (SDs) below the mean for children of the same age and sex. In adults, the condition is commonly defined as a height of 5 ft 1 in (155 cm) or less in men and 4 ft 10 in (147 cm) or less in women. Nonpathological variant short stature can be classified into three types: <u>familial short stature</u> (inherited short stature), <u>constitutional delay of growth and puberty</u> (an inherited pattern of short stature during childhood that is followed by a <u>growth spurt</u> during <u>puberty</u>, typically resulting in normal adult height), and <u>idiopathic</u> short stature (short stature in the absence of any metabolic, endocrine, or other diagnosis). These types of short stature are most often normal variants of growth and rarely affect a child's development beyond longitudinal growth. The pathological <u>causes of short stature</u> are diverse and include psychosocial circumstances as well as a variety of genetic, endocrine, and metabolic disorders, which may affect a child's development in other ways than longitudinal growth. Further diagnostic testing is indicated if a child's growth is less than what might be expected given the average height of the parents. An <u>x-ray</u> of the left hand and wrist are made to determine <u>bone age</u> (<u>skeletal age</u>), based on which the adult size of the child can be predicted. Laboratory testing can help rule out any underlying condition. Treatment is rarely indicated in nonpathological short stature (e.g., if short stature does not represent a disability to the patient), while pathological short stature is treated according to the underlying condition and usually involves <u>growth hormone</u> supplementation.

---

## Causes of short stature

Short stature can have a variety of genetic, systemic, and psychosocial causes.




* Genetic causes include:

* <u>Constitutional growth delay</u>

* <u>Laron syndrome</u>

* <u>Turner syndrome</u>

* Systemic causes include:

* <u>Congenital hypothyroidism</u>

* <u>GH</u> deficiencies

* <u>Glucocorticoid</u> excess

* Psychosocial causes include:

* Maternal substance use (e.g., <u>alcohol</u>)

* Psychosocial short stature

* Psychiatric conditions (e.g., <u>anorexia nervosa</u>)

| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Condition | Underlying cause |  | Characteristics |
| Nonpathological variant short stature |  |  |  |
| Familial short stature | <br><br>* Hereditary short stature<br><br>* Most common cause of <u>proportionate short stature</u><br><br><br> |  | <br><br>* Normal development<br><br>* <u>Skeletal age</u> consistent with chronological age<br><br><br> |
| Constitutional growth delay | <br><br>* Inherited type of <u>developmental delay</u> (<u>autosomal dominant</u>, recessive, or X-linked trait)<br><br>* Delay in pulsatile <u>hypothalamic</u> <u>GnRH</u> release<br><br><br> |  | <br><br>* Temporary delay in growth and onset of <u>puberty</u><br><br>* <u>X-ray</u> shows a delayed <u>bone age</u> (less than the individual's chronological age)<br><br>* <u>Delayed onset of puberty</u>, but no treatment is needed<br><br>* Reassuring the child and parents is sufficient.<br><br>* Catch-up growth eventually occurs.<br><br>* Individual reaches a normal adult height.<br><br><br> |
| <u>Idiopathic</u> short stature | <br>* Diagnosis of exclusion in the absence of an underlying condition<br><br> |  | <br>* Height of ≤ 2 SDs below the mean for age that cannot be explained by inheritance or pathological processes.<br><br> |
| Pathological short stature |  |  |  |

| <u>Type 1 diabetes mellitus</u> | <br>* Poor glycemic control and dysregulation of the <u>hypothalamic-pituitary-somatotropic axis</u><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Polyuria</u><br><br>* <u>Polydipsia</u><br><br>* <u>Polyphagia</u><br><br>* Recurrent infections<br><br><br> |

| Other <u>causes of short stature</u> |  |  |
| <u>Neoplasms</u> | <br><br>* <u>GH deficiency</u> due to:<br><br>* <u>Mass effect</u> of <u>hypothalamic</u> or <u>pituitary tumors</u><br><br>* <u>Hypothalamic</u> or <u>pituitary</u> radiation<br><br>* <u>Primary hypothyroidism</u> due to radiation<br><br>* <u>Nausea and vomiting</u> as a result of <u>radiotherapy</u> and <u>chemotherapy</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Weight loss<br><br>* Fatigue<br><br>* <u>Anemia</u><br><br>* <u>Fever</u><br><br><br> |

## Behavioral and psychosocial circumstances of short stature

| Psychosocial <u>causes of short stature</u> |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Condition | Underlying cause | Characteristics |
| Maternal substance use | <br><br>* <u>Nicotine</u>: tissue <u>hypoxia</u> due to an increased <u>carbon monoxide</u> concentration and release of <u>catecholamines</u><br><br>* <u>Alcohol</u>: underdevelopment of <u>skeletal muscle</u> cells and <u>central nervous system</u> (<u>fetal alcohol syndrome</u>)<br><br>* <u>Cocaine</u>: fetal <u>hypoxia</u> due to <u>placental</u> vessels <u>vasoconstriction</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Intrauterine growth retardation</u><br><br>* <u>Low birth weight</u><br><br>* Skeletal anomalies<br><br><br> |
| Psychosocial short stature | <br>* Emotional deprivation or <u>stress</u> that typically involves neglect, abuse, or a poor relationship between the patient and caregiver and leads to:<br><br>* <u>Malnutrition</u><br><br>* Low <u>GH</u> levels<br><br> | <br><br>* Poor growth or weight gain<br><br>* Poor record of school attendance and medical care<br><br>* Signs of <u>child maltreatment</u><br><br>* Clinical and radiographic signs of abuse<br><br><br> |
| <u>Anorexia nervosa</u> | <br>* <u>Malnutrition</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Low body weight<br><br>* Endocrine disorders<br><br>* <u>CNS</u> and cardiovascular abnormalities<br><br>* Recurrent bone <u>fractures</u><br><br>* Fragile <u>skin appendages</u><br><br><br> |

## Diagnosis

### <u>Patient history</u>




* <u>Physical examination</u> findings

* Growth rate

* <u>Family history</u> of short stature

* Midparental height (estimated adult height of a child calculated on the basis of parental height), calculated via the following formula:

* <u>♀</u> = [mother's height in cm + (father's height in cm - 13)]/2

* <u>♂</u> = [father's height in cm + (mother's height in cm + 13)]/2





### Laboratory tests




* <u>CBC</u>, differential blood count, <u>ESR</u>

* <u>Thyroid function tests</u> (see “<u>Hypothyroidism</u>”)

* <u>Renal function tests</u> and <u>urinalysis</u> (in case of <u>CKD</u> and associated <u>renal osteodystrophy</u>)

* Screening for <u>GH deficiency</u> (see “<u>Hypopituitarism</u>”)

* <u>Hormone</u> profile (<u>LH</u>, <u>FSH</u>, <u>estrogen</u>/<u>testosterone</u>) for <u>puberty</u> status assessment

* <u>Karyotyping</u>





### Imaging tests




* <u>X-ray</u>: : used to determine an individual's bone age and height by comparing their <u>x-ray</u> images of the nondominant hand and wrist to those displayed in the standard bone development <u>atlas</u>

* <u>Cranial</u> <u>MRI</u>: in suspicion of <u>hypothalamic</u> or <u>pituitary tumors</u>

---

## Treatment

Management depends on the underlying cause:




* Reassurance that low height is a normal variant (e.g., <u>familial short stature</u>) that does not require treatment

* Discontinuation of growth-inhibiting medication (e.g., <u>glucocorticoids</u>)

* Sex <u>hormone</u> substitution in children with <u>delayed puberty</u> and growth

* <u>GH</u> supplementation (e.g., somatropin) in cases of <u>GH deficiency</u>, <u>idiopathic</u> short stature, and <u>Turner syndrome</u>

* In case of primary severe <u>IGF-1</u> deficiency: mecasermin (recombinant <u>insulin-like growth factor</u>)

* Treatment of underlying conditions (see “<u>Causes of short stature</u>” above)
